question: Q-A1
claim: Velut et al. 2017 outward-striking one-mass lip model: h'' + (w_l/Q_l) h' + w_l^2 (h - h0) = (p_b - p(t))/mu (eq. 1), Bernoulli flow u = W h sqrt(2(p_b - p)/rho) (eq. 5), impedance as sum of complex modes Z(w) = Zc sum_n [C_n/(jw - s_n) + C_n*/(jw - s_n*)] (eq. 3), with modal ODEs dp_n/dt = Zc C_n u + s_n p_n and p = 2 sum Re(p_n) (eq. 4).

sources.title: How well can linear stability analysis predict the behaviour of an outward-striking valve brass instrument model? (Velut, Vergez, Gilbert, Djahanbani), Acta Acust. united Acust. 103(1):132-148
sources.locator: Sec. 2.1, eqs. (1)-(8), pp. 4-6 of HAL version

notes: Eq.(1): d2h/dt2 + (wl/Ql) dh/dt + wl^2 (h - h0) = (1/mu)(pb - p(t)); wl = 2 pi fl; mu = lip surface-mass equivalent (kg/m^2). Eq.(2) Z = P/U. Eq.(3) Z(w) = Zc * sum_{n=1..N} [Cn/(jw - sn) + Cn*/(jw - sn*)], Zc = rho c / S with S the input cross-section at the mouthpiece rim. Eq.(4) dpn/dt = Zc Cn u(t) + sn pn, p(t) = 2 sum_n Re(pn). Eq.(5) u(t) = sqrt(2/rho) * W * h(t) * sqrt(pb - p(t)), rho = 1.19 kg/m^3 at 20 C, W = lip channel width. Eqs.(6)-(8) state-space form X = [h, dh/dt, {pn}]. Jet assumed laminar in lip channel, turbulent in mouthpiece, no pressure recovery. Mouth pressure pb treated as constant (vocal tract ignored). Velut uses a trombone (Courtois T149) with 18-mode fit, not a trumpet. Practical implementation note (from Freour 2020 eq. 2 and Doc 2023 eq. 4): use u = b*sqrt(2|p0-p|/rho)*sign(p0-p)*max(h,0) to handle reverse flow and lip closure.

question: Q-A3
claim: A one-mass outward-striking model CAN produce a pedal-like note well above the strongly inharmonic first resonance: for the trombone Velut et al. find f_thresh,1 = 55.6 Hz vs f_ac,1 = 38 Hz (ratio 1.46, close to Bb1 = 58.27 Hz) at f_l = 49 Hz, and time-domain simulation at p_b = 150 Pa gives 61.86 Hz; a single-mode resonator still gives 61.06 Hz, so the pedal is attributed to coupling with the first mode, not the privileged-frequency mechanism of upper modes.

Signal Processing 4(1):79-87) proposed a new algorithm for nonlinear propagation applied to a trumpet model, Msallam et al. 2000 (Acta Acust. 86(4):725-736) a trombone model with nonlinear propagation in the cylindrical part, and Helie & Smet 2008 a real-time 'brassy' audio effect for a straight pipe; none of these full texts were accessible, so the algorithm details below are derived from eq. sources.locator: Introduction refs [8]-[10] (bibliographic data)

notes: Implementable scheme (derived from the exact implicit solution of eq. (2), Poisson/Earnshaw simple wave, valid before shock formation): output at the end of an equivalent cylinder of length Leq: p_out(t) = p_in(t - Leq/c0 + beta Leq p_in / (rho0 c0^3)) evaluated implicitly, i.e. each input sample s_k = p_in(t_k) arrives at time t_k + Leq/c0 - beta Leq s_k/(rho0 c0^3): positive pressure arrives early. Real-time realisation = amplitude-dependent fractional delay / time warping: compute arrival times for incoming samples, resample onto the uniform output grid (monotonic as long as Leq < x_s; when arrival times would cross, a shock has formed - apply weak-shock rule or simply limit dp/dt/oversample and low-pass). Delta delay for p = 10 kPa, Leq = 0.85 m: beta Leq p/(rho c^3) = 1.2*0.85*1e4/(1.2*4.04e7) = 0.21 ms (~9 samples at 44.1 kHz). Add wall losses as a linear low-pass/fractional (sqrt(jw)) filter in series, split into a few segments (operator splitting as in Berjamin et al. 2017). Berjamin uses a TVD finite-volume scheme + diffusive approximation of the fractional integral (too slow for real time: 18 min per simulated second). Berjamin results: nonlinear propagation raised playing frequency by up to 45 Hz (+157 cents) in transients, and altered thresholds/register behaviour - output-side-only modelling (no feedback) ignores these effects.
